claim: Stereotyped facial movements reveal people's happiness, surprise, fear, anger, disgust, and sadness in a way that can be easily interpreted by their congeners.
source: Stereotyped facial movements – facial expressions – reveal people's happiness, surprise, fear, anger, disgust, and sadness in a way that can be easily interpreted by their congeners (Ekman, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ekman, 1982.

claim: The ability to express and recognize facial expressions is crucial for social interactions.
source: The ability to express and recognize facial expressions is crucial for social interactions (Elfenbein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Elfenbein et al., 2007.

claim: Three types of representations are necessary and sufficient for efficient visual recognition of facial expression: (1) a series of progressively more abstract visuo-perceptual representations of the postures and movements of the observed face; (2) stored structural descriptions of the features characterizing known facial expressions; and (3) the conceptual/semantic representations that characterize the facial expressions.
source: Three types of representations are necessary and sufficient for efficient visual recognition of facial expression: (1) a series of progressively more abstract visuo-perceptual representations of the postures and movements of the observed face; (2) stored structural descriptions of the features characterizing known facial expressions; and (3) the conceptual/semantic representations that characterize the facial expressions (e.g., Bruce and Young, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bruce and Young, 1986.

claim: An alternative view suggests that efficient facial expression recognition cannot be achieved by visual analysis alone but requires a process of motor simulation.
source: In the last 20 years, an alternative view suggesting that efficient (i.e., fast and accurate) facial expression recognition cannot be achieved by visual analysis alone but requires a process of motor simulation – an unconscious, covert imitation of the observed facial postures or movements – has gained considerable prominence (Goldman and Sripada, 2005; Ipser and Cook, 2016; Montgomery and Haxby, 2008; Niedenthal et al., 2010; Pitcher et al., 2008; Paracampo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Goldman and Sripada, 2005; Ipser and Cook, 2016; Montgomery and Haxby, 2008; Niedenthal et al., 2010; Pitcher et al., 2008; Paracampo et al., 2017.

claim: The motor view has become increasingly influential in neuroscience, philosophy, neurology and psychiatry where it is suggested that it opens new clinical perspectives for the diagnosis, understanding and rehabilitation of clinical populations presenting with facial expression recognition deficits such as Parkinson's disease, autism, and schizophrenia.
source: This 'motor' view has become increasingly influential in neuroscience, philosophy, neurology and psychiatry where it is suggested that it opens new clinical perspectives for the diagnosis, understanding and rehabilitation of clinical populations presenting with facial expression recognition deficits such as Parkinson's disease (Ricciardi et al., 2017), autism (Dapretto et al., 2006; Gordon et al., 2014), and schizophrenia (Torregrossa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ricciardi et al., 2017; Dapretto et al., 2006; Gordon et al., 2014; Torregrossa et al., 2019.

claim: Neuroimaging studies and studies combining transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the motor cortex and electromyographic recording of facial muscles have reported that viewing a facial expression activates parts of the motor system, which are also involved in executing that facial expression.
source: First, neuroimaging studies and studies combining transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the motor cortex and electromyographic recording of facial muscles have reported that viewing a facial expression activates parts of the motor system, which are also involved in executing that facial expression (Carr et al., 2003; Dimberg, 1982; Dimberg et al., 2000; Hess and Blairy, 2001; Leslie et al., 2004; Montgomery and Haxby, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carr et al., 2003; Dimberg, 1982; Dimberg et al., 2000; Hess and Blairy, 2001; Leslie et al., 2004; Montgomery and Haxby, 2008.

claim: Performance in tasks involving facial expression recognition can be modulated by experimental manipulations of the normal state of the observers' motor system, such as concurrent motor tasks or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the motor cortex.
source: Second, performance in tasks involving facial expression recognition can be modulated by experimental manipulations of the normal state of the observers' motor system, such as concurrent motor tasks or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the motor cortex (Ipser and Cook, 2016; Maringer et al., 2011; Oberman et al., 2007; Paracampo et al., 2017; Ponari et al., 2012; Rychlowska et al., 2014; Wood et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ipser and Cook, 2016; Maringer et al., 2011; Oberman et al., 2007; Paracampo et al., 2017; Ponari et al., 2012; Rychlowska et al., 2014; Wood et al., 2016.

claim: Several studies have reported that individuals with Moebius Syndrome scored below average in facial expression recognition experiments.
source: Several studies have reported, for instance, that individuals with Moebius Syndrome, an extremely rare congenital nonprogressive condition (Verzijl et al., 2003) resulting in facial paralysis (usually complete and bilateral), scored below average in facial expression recognition experiments (Bate et al., 2013; Calder et al., 2000; Giannini et al., 1984; Nicolini et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bate et al., 2013; Calder et al., 2000; Giannini et al., 1984; Nicolini et al., 2019.

claim: Co-occurrence of facial expression production and recognition disorders have been reported in Parkinson's and in Huntington's disease.
source: Co-occurrence of facial expression production and recognition disorders have also been reported in Parkinson's (Ricciardi et al., 2017) and in Huntington's disease (Trinkler et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ricciardi et al., 2017 and Trinkler et al., 2013.

claim: The activation of the motor system during the observation of facial expressions could result from a mere reaction of the observer to others' facial expression after it has been recognized as an instance of a given emotion.
source: The activation of the motor system during the observation of facial expressions could result from a mere reaction (e.g., emotional contagion or a way to signal empathy) of the observer to others' facial expression after it has been recognized as an instance of a given emotion (Hess et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hess et al., 2014.

claim: Motor system activation during facial expression observation may result from visuo-motor transformations serving other purposes than facial expression recognition such as working memory encoding or mimicry in order to foster affiliative goals.
source: It may also result from visuo-motor transformations serving other purposes than facial expression recognition such as working memory encoding (Vannuscorps and Caramazza, 2016a) or mimicry in order to foster affiliative goals (Fischer and Hess, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vannuscorps and Caramazza, 2016a and Fischer and Hess, 2017.

claim: TMS applied to an area may have distant effects on other areas to which it projects.
source: TMS applied to an area may have distant effects on other areas to which it projects (Papeo et al., 2015; Ruff et al., 2009; Siebner et al., 2009; Siebner and Rothwell, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Papeo et al., 2015; Ruff et al., 2009; Siebner et al., 2009; Siebner and Rothwell, 2003.

claim: The motor cortex projects to the visual cortex involved in the perception of biological motion in order to support the control of one's body movements.
source: The motor cortex projects to the visual cortex involved in the perception of biological motion in order to support the control of one's body movements (Wolpert et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wolpert et al., 2003.

claim: The visual cortex involved in the perception of body parts shows increased activity when moving these body parts even in the absence of visual feedback.
source: the visual cortex involved in the perception of body parts shows increased activity when moving these body parts even in the absence of visual feedback (Astafiev et al., 2004; Dinstein et al., 2007; Orlov et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Astafiev et al., 2004; Dinstein et al., 2007; Orlov et al., 2010.

claim: The finding that visual information about lip movements influences auditory speech perception does not imply that auditory speech perception requires the visual system.
source: For instance, the finding that visual information about lip movements influences auditory speech perception does not imply that auditory speech perception requires the visual system and has never been presented as a proof of this (McGurk and MacDonald, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McGurk and MacDonald, 1976.

claim: Results showing that auditory information affects the efficiency of facial expression recognition have been interpreted as evidence that available auditory or context information can influence facial expression recognition, but not that the auditory system is critical for efficient facial expression recognition.
source: Likewise, results showing that auditory information affects the efficiency of facial expression recognition have been interpreted as evidence that available auditory or context information can influence facial expression recognition, but not that the auditory system is critical for efficient facial expression recognition (Collignon et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Collignon et al., 2008.

claim: In a study of 108 patients with focal brain lesions, Adolphs et al., 2000 found no association between the ability to recognize facial expressions and motor lesions/impairment.
source: In line with this possibility, in a study of 108 patients with focal brain lesions, Adolphs et al., 2000 found no association between the ability to recognize facial expressions and motor lesions/impairment.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Adolphs et al., 2000.

claim: Moebius syndrome typically impacts not only the individuals' sensorimotor system, but also their visual, perceptual, cognitive, and social abilities.
source: Likewise, Moebius syndrome typically impacts not only the individuals' sensorimotor system, but also their visual, perceptual, cognitive, and social abilities (Bate et al., 2013; Carta et al., 2011; Gillberg and Steffenburg, 1989; Johansson et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bate et al., 2013; Carta et al., 2011; Gillberg and Steffenburg, 1989; Johansson et al., 2007.

claim: In Bate et al., 2013 study, five out of six participants with Moebius Syndrome were impaired in at least one of three facial expression recognition tasks.
source: In a study by Bate et al., 2013, for instance, five out of six participants with Moebius Syndrome were impaired in at least one of three facial expression recognition tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bate et al., 2013.

claim: The same five individuals with Moebius Syndrome who were impaired in facial expression recognition were also impaired in their ability to recognize facial identity and/or in tests assessing low-level vision and object recognition.
source: However, the same five individuals were also impaired in their ability to recognize facial identity and/or in tests assessing low-level vision and object recognition indicating that the facial expression recognition impairment cannot unambiguously be associated with the facial paralysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the study by Bate et al., 2013.

claim: There are reports of individuals with Moebius Syndrome who achieve a normal level of performance in facial expression recognition despite their congenital facial paralysis.
source: In favor of the view that recognition does not require motor simulation, there are reports of individuals with Moebius Syndrome (IMS) who achieve a normal level of performance in facial expression recognition despite their congenital facial paralysis (Bate et al., 2013; Calder et al., 2000; Rives Bogart and Matsumoto, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bate et al., 2013; Calder et al., 2000; Rives Bogart and Matsumoto, 2010.

claim: One individual with Moebius Syndrome (MB4) performed very close to the average level of performance of the controls in three facial expression recognition tests despite having facial movements restricted to slight puckering of the mouth bilaterally.
source: For instance, in contrast to the five other MS participants from Bate et al.'s study (2103) cited above, one IMS (the only one who obtained normal scores in facial identity recognition, object recognition and low-level vision tests, MB4) performed very close to the average level of performance of the controls in three facial expression recognition tests (the Ekman 60 faces test, the Emotion Hexagon test, and the Reading the Mind in the Eyes test) despite having facial movements restricted to slight puckering of the mouth bilaterally.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bate et al., 2013.

claim: In Rives Bogart and Matsumoto, 2010 study, the performance of 37 IMS participants was comparable to that of 37 control participants in a task in which they viewed pictures of one of seven emotions and were asked to select the corresponding emotion from a list of the alternatives.
source: In Rives Bogart and Matsumoto, 2010 study, the performance of 37 IMS participants was comparable to that of 37 control participants in a task in which they viewed pictures of one of seven emotions (anger, contempt, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise) and were asked to select the corresponding emotion from a list of the alternatives.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rives Bogart and Matsumoto, 2010.

claim: It has been suggested that a mild or subtle deficit in facial expression recognition may have gone undetected in previous studies of individuals with Moebius Syndrome because they relied mostly on untimed picture labelling tasks.
source: Although these findings undermine the hypothesis that facial expression recognition requires motor simulation, it has been suggested that a mild or subtle deficit in facial expression recognition may have gone undetected in these studies because they relied mostly on untimed picture labelling tasks (De Stefani et al., 2019; Van Rysewyk, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to De Stefani et al., 2019 and Van Rysewyk, 2011.

claim: The controls' performance was significantly above chance in all five facial expression recognition experiments.
source: The results of these analyses showed that the controls' data were indeed significantly above chance (all t-tests > 8)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-tests) of the control participants' data.

claim: The controls' data were normally distributed in all five facial expression experiments.
source: and normally distributed in all five facial expression experiments (all five Ws > 0.930, all ps > 0.13).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Shapiro-Wilk tests) of the control participants' data.

claim: The control participants' average performance in Experiment four was significantly better than that reported in the only other study reporting the results of the same (French) version of the task.
source: One-sample t-tests indicated that our control participants' average performance (M = 28.6; SD = 2.4) in Experiment four was significantly better than that reported in the only other study reporting the results of the same (French) version of the task (M = 24.8; SD = 3.8; t (24)=7.9; Prevost et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (one-sample t-test) with data from Prevost et al., 2014.

claim: The control group performed slightly better in Experiment 3 than the average performance of the three comparable age groups reported in a previous study using the same task.
source: Our control group also performed slightly better (M = 63.04, SD = 10.22) than the average performance of the three comparable age groups reported in a previous study using the task of Experiment 3 (M = 62.6, SD = 9.6; t (24)<0.2; Kessels et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (one-sample t-test) with data from Kessels et al., 2014.

claim: The control sample performed lower in the Amusement from Smiles experiment than the performance expected from Paracampo et al., 2017 norming study.
source: Our control sample performed lower than the performance expected from Paracampo et al., 2017 norming study of the Amusement from Smiles experiment (66% in our study vs 75%).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with data from Paracampo et al., 2017.

claim: The experiment included only half the number of trials of the original Amusement from Smiles experiment, offering less perceptual learning opportunity to the participants.
source: However, our experiment included only half the number of trials of the original experiment (Paracampo et al., 2017) offering less perceptual learning opportunity to our participants (Huelle et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with the original experiment and a citation to Huelle et al., 2014.

claim: IMS 8 and 10 performed the five experiments with normotypical efficiency.
source: These analyses indicated that IMS 8 and 10, displayed in green and yellow in Figure 1, performed the five experiments with normotypical efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (Crawford and Howell modified t-tests) and Figure 1.

claim: There was no evidence that IMS 8 and 10 performed facial expression recognition tasks less efficiently than facial identity recognition or emotional speech recognition tasks.
source: All the comparisons were either clearly not significant (3/30 comparisons, all BSDTs > 0.6) or indicated a comparatively better performance in facial expression recognition tasks than in the control tasks (27/30 comparisons). Thus, there was no evidence that IMS 8 and 10 performed facial expression recognition tasks less efficiently than facial identity recognition or emotional speech recognition tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (Bayesian Standardized Difference Tests).

claim: The response matrices of IMS 8 and 10 were highly correlated with those of control participants when all responses were considered in Experiments 1-3.
source: The resulting correlation coefficients were very high both when all responses were considered (all three Pearson's Rs (36)>0.95; all ps < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (Pearson correlations) of response matrices.

claim: The response matrices of IMS 8 and 10 were highly correlated with those of control participants when only errors were considered in Experiments 1-3.
source: and when only errors were considered (all three Pearson's Rs (30)>0.63; all ps < 0.001), indicating that the groups consistently confused the same set of alternatives.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (Pearson correlations) of error patterns.

claim: The confusion matrices of the other IMS were also strongly correlated to that of the control participants.
source: Note that the confusion matrices of the other IMS were also strongly correlated to that of the control participants (all three Pearson's Rs (36)>0.95; all ps < 0.001; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (Pearson correlations) and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: IMS 8 was able to execute a mild combined backward/upward movement of the right angle of the mouth, a slight backward movement of the left angle of the mouth, a slight contraction of the mentalis and some slight movements of the upper eye lids.
source: IMS eight was able to execute a mild combined backward/upward movement of the right angle of the mouth, a slight backward movement of the left angle of the mouth, a slight contraction of the mentalis and some slight movements of the upper eye lids.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical examination of IMS 8's facial movements.

claim: IMS10 was only able to execute a slight bilateral movement of the angles of the mouth backwards and downwards and some up and down movements of the superior eye lids.
source: IMS10 was only able to execute a slight bilateral movement of the angles of the mouth backwards and downwards and some up and down movements of the superior eye lids.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical examination of IMS 10's facial movements.

claim: The facial movements that IMS 8 and 10 were able to execute covered only a small part of the facial movements that would be required to imitate the different facial expressions of emotions.
source: Importantly, however, these movements covered only a small part of the facial movements that would be required to imitate the different facial expressions of emotions (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of observed movements with requirements for facial expression imitation.

claim: The facial movements of IMS 8 and 10 were largely the same when they attempted to imitate the different facial expressions.
source: and they were largely the same when they attempted to imitate the different facial expressions (sadness, happiness, anger, surprise, disgust, fear, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Control participants were unable to recognize video-clips showing the two IMS attempting to imitate the six same facial expressions.
source: Control participants were unable to recognize video-clips showing the two IMS attempting to imitate the six same facial expressions (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The facial movements that the IMS were able to execute are small in amplitude, very limited in types, and do not discriminate different facial expressions.
source: In sum, the facial movements that the IMS were able to execute are small in amplitude, very limited in types, and do not discriminate different facial expressions.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from the clinical and experimental observations of IMS facial movements.

claim: IMS 10 was among the participants with the most severe facial paralysis.
source: This was clearly not the case: IMS 10 was among the participants with the most severe facial paralysis (see Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The performance of the IMS who performed more poorly than controls in Experiments 1–3 was strongly and significantly correlated with their respective performance on the mid-level perception screening test.
source: Instructively, and by contrast, the performance of the IMS who performed more poorly than controls in Experiments 1–3 was strongly and significantly correlated with their respective performance on the mid-level perception screening test (three rs > 0.5, ps < 0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (correlations).

claim: 7/9 of the IMS participants who failed to meet the criteria for normotypical efficient facial expression recognition obtained also equally weak or weaker performance in the facial identity and/or the emotional speech recognition task.
source: and 7/9 of the IMS participants (IMS1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9) who failed to meet the criteria for normotypical efficient facial expression recognition obtained also equally weak or weaker performance in the facial identity and/or the emotional speech recognition task (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The IMS's performance variability seems to be at least partly due to associated visual and/or cognitive disorders, rather than to their facial paralysis.
source: Thus, the IMS's performance variability seems to be at least partly due to associated visual and/or cognitive disorders, rather than to their facial paralysis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the correlation between facial expression recognition performance and performance on other visual/cognitive tasks.

claim: One-way ANCOVAs failed to reveal any significant effect of Group in Experiments 1, 2, 4 and 5 when controlling for performance in Experiments 6–8.
source: In line with the possibility that the IMS's performance variability is likely due to associated visual and/or cognitive disorders rather than to their facial paralysis, these analyses failed to reveal any significant effect of Group in Experiments 1, 2, 4 and 5 (all Fs <1; all ps > 0.37).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (one-way ANCOVAs).

claim: Only IMS1 performed significantly less well in Experiment five than in the three control experiments.
source: Only IMS1 performed significantly less well in Experiment five than in the three control experiments (Experiments 6–8).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (Bayesian Standardized Difference Tests).

claim: Several IMS failed to recognize facial expressions as efficiently as control participants in one or several experiments.
source: As in previous studies (Bate et al., 2013; Calder et al., 2000; Giannini et al., 1984; Nicolini et al., 2019), several IMS failed to recognize facial expressions as efficiently as control participants in one (IMS 1, 3, 5, 7) or several (IMS 2, 6, 9, 11) experiments (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Two of the IMS (IMS 8 and 10) fulfilled the criteria for 'normotypical efficient facial expression recognition'.
source: Nevertheless, and more interestingly, we also found that two of the IMS (IMS 8 and 10) fulfilled the criteria for 'normotypical efficient facial expression recognition': (1) they both scored above 0.85 standard deviations below the mean of the controls in all five facial expression recognition experiments; (2) they performed as well in these tasks as in other face-related visual tasks (face identity) and emotion recognition tasks (vocal emotion recognition); and (3) they performed these tasks in a way that is qualitatively similar to the controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses and qualitative comparisons.

claim: IMS 8 and 10 had severe facial paralysis.
source: These two IMS had severe facial paralysis.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical examination data.

claim: IMS 8 and 10 could not execute most of the facial movements that would be required to imitate the different facial expressions of emotions.
source: They could not execute most of the facial movements that would be required to imitate the different facial expressions of emotions (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on clinical examination and comparison with requirements for facial expression imitation.

claim: The findings constitute existence proof that it is possible to account for efficient facial expression recognition without having to invoke a mechanism of 'motor simulation'.
source: These dissociations challenge the central premise of the models of facial expression recognition centered on facial mimicry: they constitute existence proof that it is possible to account for efficient facial expression recognition without having to invoke a mechanism of 'motor simulation', even in very sensitive and challenging tasks requiring, for instance, the identification of a facial expression in 150 milliseconds, only from information available in the eye region, when the stimuli are morphs composed of a mixture of emotions, and when the task involves discriminating fake versus genuine smiles.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental findings showing normotypical performance in IMS 8 and 10.

claim: The observation that IMS 8 and 10 performed the facial recognition tasks in a qualitatively similar manner to the controls makes it unlikely that they developed an atypically efficient visual system to compensate for their congenital paralysis.
source: However, the observation that these IMS performed the facial recognition tasks in a qualitatively similar manner to the controls makes this unlikely.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the qualitative analysis of performance patterns.

claim: Facial expression recognition is better explained by the perceptual-cognitive view according to which it is supported by visuo-perceptual, structural and conceptual, but not sensorimotor, representations.
source: At this juncture, facial expression recognition is thus better explained by the perceptual-cognitive view according to which it is supported by visuo-perceptual, structural and conceptual, but not sensorimotor, representations.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and theoretical considerations.

claim: Eleven individuals with severe to complete facial paralysis in the context of the Moebius Syndrome were tested.
source: We tested eleven individuals with severe to complete facial paralysis in the context of the Moebius Syndrome (IMS participants; eight females; all right-handed; various education levels; mean age ± SD: 27.7 ± 9.25 years)
evidence: The claim describes the participant sample.

claim: The performance of IMS participants was compared to that of 25 typically developed highly educated young adults.
source: and compared their performance to that of 25 typically developed highly educated young adults (15 females; three left-handed; all college students or graduates without any history of psychiatric or neurological disorder; Mean age ± SD: 28.6 ± 6.5 years).
evidence: The claim describes the control participant sample.

claim: All IMS were able to speak intelligibly and to convey emotions in their speech.
source: All IMS were able to speak intelligibly and to convey emotions in their speech.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observation.

claim: The study was approved by the biomedical ethics committee of the Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, Brussels, Belgium.
source: The study was approved by the biomedical ethics committee of the Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, Brussels, Belgium and all participants gave written informed consent prior to the study.
evidence: The claim states an administrative fact about the study.

claim: Participants performed five facial expression recognition tasks, two facial identity recognition tasks, and an emotional speech recognition task.
source: Participants performed five facial expression recognition tasks, two facial identity recognition tasks, and an emotional speech recognition task.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design.

claim: In Experiments 1 and 2, participants viewed a picture of an actor's face expressing one of six facial expressions presented for either 150 ms or 1 s between two pictures of the same actor displaying a neutral expression.
source: In each of the 60 trials of Experiments 1 and 2, participants viewed a picture of an actor's face expressing one of six facial expressions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise; Lundqvist et al., 1998) presented for either 150 ms (Experiment 1) or 1 s (Experiment 2) between two pictures of the same actor displaying a neutral expression (presented for 1 s each).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure for Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: In Experiment 3, participants viewed 96 video clips depicting an actor's face expressing one of the six basic emotions at one of four different levels of intensity and had to associate it with its corresponding label among six alternatives.
source: In Experiment 3, participants viewed 96 video clips depicting an actor's face expressing one of the six basic emotions at one of four different levels of intensity (40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%; Kessels et al., 2014; Montagne et al., 2007) and had to associate it with its corresponding label among six alternatives.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure for Experiment 3.

claim: The experimental paradigm used in Experiment 3 has been shown to be sensitive to subtle emotion recognition disorders in clinical conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder, amygdalectomy and social phobia.
source: This experimental paradigm has been shown to be sensitive to subtle emotion recognition disorders in clinical conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (Poljac et al., 2011), amygdalectomy (Ammerlaan et al., 2008) and social phobia (Montagne et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Poljac et al., 2011; Ammerlaan et al., 2008; Montagne et al., 2006.

claim: In Experiment 4, participants were asked to associate a picture depicting the eye-region of someone's face to the verbal label that best described that person's emotion or mental state among four subtly different alternatives.
source: In Experiment 4, we tested the ability to recognize more complex mental states (e.g., skeptical, insisting, suspicious) from information restricted to the actor's eye region. On each of the 36 trials of this experiment (the 'Reading the Mind in the Eyes' test Revised version; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), participants were asked to associate a picture depicting the eye-region of someone's face to the verbal label that best described that person's emotion or mental state (e.g., skeptical, insisting, suspicious) among four subtly different alternatives.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure for Experiment 4.

claim: Performance in Experiment 4 has been shown to be affected by botulinum toxin injections on the forehead, oxytocin administration, and hampered in persons with autism, schizophrenia, anorexia nervosa, depression, Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease.
source: Performance in this experiment has been previously shown to be sensitive to both subtle experimental modulations of the observers' motor system and slight emotion recognition disorders in clinical conditions: It is affected by botulinum toxin (Botox) injections on the forehead (Neal and Chartrand, 2011), oxytocin administration (Domes et al., 2007), and hampered in persons with autism (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), schizophrenia (Kettle et al., 2008), anorexia nervosa (Harrison et al., 2010), depression (Szanto et al., 2012), Parkinson's disease (Tsuruya et al., 2011) and Huntington's disease (Allain et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In Experiment 5, participants viewed a video clip showing an actor who was either spontaneously smiling out of amusement or producing a forced smile and had to discriminate genuine from fake smiles.
source: Experiment five tested the hypothesis that motor simulation is particularly important for the ability to discriminate fake versus genuine smiles (e.g., Paracampo et al., 2017). In each of the 32 trials of this experiment, participants viewed a video clip showing an actor who was either spontaneously smiling out of amusement (genuine smile) or producing a forced (fake) smile and had to use subtle morphological and dynamic features of the smile in order to discriminate genuine from fake smiles (Ekman, 1982; Krumhuber and Manstead, 2009; Paracampo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure for Experiment 5.

claim: Performance in the Amusement from Smiles task is influenced by simple procedures such as wearing a mouth guard, TMS in the face sensorimotor cortex, and vowel articulation.
source: Performance in the Amusement from Smiles task is influenced by simple procedures such as wearing a mouth guard (Rychlowska et al., 2014), TMS in the face sensorimotor cortex (Paracampo et al., 2017), and vowel articulation (Ipser and Cook, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rychlowska et al., 2014; Paracampo et al., 2017; Ipser and Cook, 2016.

claim: Experiment 6 used the Cambridge Face Memory Test (CFMT).
source: Experiments 6 and 7 tested participants' facial identity recognition skills. Experiment six used the Cambridge Face Memory Test (CFMT; Duchaine and Nakayama, 2006)
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure for Experiment 6.

claim: In Experiment 7, participants were presented with a target face and six pictures morphed to contain different proportions of the target face and were asked to sort them from most like to least like the target face.
source: In each of the 8 trials of Experiment 7 – the Cambridge Face Perception Test (CFPT; Duchaine et al., 2007) – participants were presented with a target face and, below it, six pictures morphed to contain different proportions of the target face (28%, 40%, 52%, 64%, 76% and 88%) and were asked to sort them from most like to least like the target face.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure for Experiment 7.

claim: In Experiment 8, participants were asked to listen to audio-clips in which a speaker simulated one of seven emotions while producing a sentence in a language that none of the participants understood and to pick its corresponding label.
source: Experiment eight tested participants' ability to recognize emotions from emotional speech. In each of the 60 trials of this experiment, participants were asked to listen to a ~ 2 s long audio-clip in which a female or a male speaker simulated one of seven emotions (anger, anxiety/fear, boredom, disgust, happiness, sadness, neutral) while producing a sentence which could be applied to any emotion in a language that none of the IMS or control participants declared to understand (in German; from Burkhardt et al., 2005). Participants were asked to listen carefully to the audio-clips and, then, to pick its corresponding label presented among the six other alternatives.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure for Experiment 8.

claim: The participants with Moebius Syndrome participated in a motor examination which included imitation of facial movements involving specific muscles on the territory of the facial nerve.
source: The participants with Moebius Syndrome additionally participated to a motor, which included three main parts: (1) They were asked to imitate facial movements involving specific muscles on the territory of the facial nerve: the buccinator (pressing cheeks on the side of the teeth and pull back the angle of the mouth), zigomaticus major (large smile), risorius (draw the angle of the mouth straight backwards), levator anguli oris (pulling the angle of the mouth upward), depressor anguli oris (pulling the angle of the mouth downward), levator labii superioris (raise and protrude the upper lips), depressor labii inferioris (pull the lower lip and angle of the mouth down), the mentalis (protrude the lower lip and make a pouting face), the frontalis (elevate the eyebrows), the corrigator supercilia and depressor supercilia (frown), orbicularis oculi (close the eyes gently, close the eyes tightly), and the procerus and nasalis (wrinkle the nose) muscles.
evidence: The claim describes the motor examination procedure.

claim: The motor examination tested the trigeminal and hypoglossal nerves by asking participants to produce various facial movements upon verbal command.
source: (2) In order to test the trigeminal and hypoglossal nerves, we asked them to produce various facial other movements upon verbal command: opening and closing the jaws, moving the tongue from left to right, up and down, back and forth, and articulating repeatedly the syllable/pa/for 5–6 s.
evidence: The claim describes part of the motor examination procedure.

claim: The motor examination included asking participants to imitate six facial expressions based on picture examples.
source: (3) In order to document their ability to execute facial expressions, they were asked to imitate as well as possible six facial expressions (happiness, anger, fear, disgust, sadness and surprise) based on a picture example from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces set (Actress AF01, front view; Lundqvist, D., Flykt, A., and Öhman, A., 1998).
evidence: The claim describes part of the motor examination procedure.

claim: The performance of IMS participants during motor examination tasks was recorded and analyzed offline.
source: Their performance during these tasks was recorded and analyzed offline. The results of these analyses are presented on Table 1.
evidence: The claim describes the data collection and analysis procedure.

claim: Individuals can achieve normotypical efficient facial expression recognition despite a congenital absence of relevant facial motor representations.
source: we demonstrate that individuals can achieve normotypical efficient facial expression recognition despite a congenital absence of relevant facial motor representations and, therefore, unaided by motor simulation.
evidence: The claim is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from IMS 8 and 10.

claim: The findings underscore the need to reconsider the role of motor simulation in facial expression recognition.
source: This underscores the need to reconsider the role of motor simulation in facial expression recognition.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.
